concepts.title: The Flattering Letter and the Fatal Invitation
concepts.definition: A young, impecunious writer receives a fan letter from a lady praising his work; flattered, he replies, and she invites herself to a luncheon at Foyot's -- a restaurant of the wealthy -- saying she takes nothing for lunch. Too young to refuse a reader, he budgets the month's rent on the meal.
concepts.key_idea: Vanity accepts what sense would refuse -- one lunch ordered against a whole month's rent.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww108.txt opening sections (fan letter from the lady, foyot's restaurant, she takes nothing for lunch, the writer's tight budget)
question_patterns: why does the writer agree to lunch with the lady
in class 11 the luncheon: why is foyot's an expensive choice
what did the lady say about her lunching habits
how much could the writer afford for the meal
describe the letter that began the whole episode
what does the story suggest about the writer's vanity

solution_steps.explain: Her praise of his book touches his young vanity -- the wound he cannot resist.
She proposes Foyot's, the luxury restaurant, while insisting she never eats luncheon -- a warning unheeded.
He sets aside what should carry him through the month -- the story's stakes are fixed at the table.

concepts.title: Ordering While Professing Abstinence
concepts.definition: The lady declares she never eats more than one thing, and then orders salmon, caviare, asparagus, a peach and champagne and coffee -- while the guest confines himself to the cheapest mutton chop and water. Each new order widens the gap between her profession and her plate, and his panic grows with the bill.
concepts.key_idea: One thing for lunch -- said while ordering everything else on the menu.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww108.txt ordering scenes (salmon, caviare, asparagus, peach, champagne coffee, mutton chop and water for the narrator, growing bill and panic)
question_patterns: list the things the lady orders during the luncheon
in class 11 the luncheon: what does the narrator order for himself and why
how does the gap between the lady's words and actions create humour
why does the narrator panic as the meal progresses
comment on the lady's statement that she never eats more than one thing
trace the rising bill through the courses of the meal

solution_steps.explain: Salmon with caviare, asparagus, peach and champagne-coffee arrive course by course, each beyond his means.
He answers each course by ordering the cheapest chop and water, his heart sinking as the bill climbs.
Her repeated claims of abstinence against her growing appetite is Maugham's sustained comic irony.

concepts.title: Revenge at Last: Remembering the Luncheon
concepts.definition: The writer leaves with a whole month before him and no money. Years later, meeting her at a play, now enormous in girth, he has his revenge at last: when she names fish as her only food, he asks, with perfect dryness, whether she remembers the fatal luncheon.
concepts.key_idea: Revenge served without a word -- time itself turns her 'one thing' into the story's final laugh.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww108.txt ending sections (meeting at the play, her enormous size, fish as her only food, the narrator's retort, revenge motif)
question_patterns: how does the narrator get his revenge at the end
in class 11 the luncheon: why is the last line of the story amusing
what has happened to the lady when the writer meets her again
explain the significance of the word fish in the ending
is the narrator's revenge justified discuss
comment on maugham's use of irony throughout the story

solution_steps.explain: Years on, at a first night, the vastly enlarged lady greets him warmly as her discovery.
She repeats her old line -- that she takes nothing but one thing, fish.
He asks whether she remembers that luncheon -- and her appetite answers what she will not.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Show how Maugham builds the humour of the luncheon scene through the contrast between speech and action.

solution_template.explain: The lady insists she never eats anything for luncheon, or just one small thing.
Each insistence is followed by another expensive order -- salmon, caviare, asparagus, peach.
The comedy lives in the widening gap between her words and her plate, with the narrator's panic as chorus.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the narrator not remind the lady of the unpaid luncheon when they meet again?

solution_template.explain: He never mentions the debt directly -- a direct accusation would cost him dignity, not her.
He waits for her own words -- fish, her only food -- to summon the memory for both of them.
The wittiest revenge needs no accusation; her figure and her phrase together settle the account.
